title: GFS: a file system built for machines that break
dek: In 2003 a search company described how it stored a copy of the web on hundreds of cheap machines that failed every day. One master that only answers small questions, 64 MB chunks kept three times, and a relaxed idea of consistency: the design behind a decade of big-data storage.

items: GFS stores huge files across hundreds of ordinary machines and treats failure as normal, not rare: with that many disks, something is always broken.
One master keeps all the metadata in memory and only answers small questions. The data moves directly between clients and chunkservers, in 64 MB chunks with three copies each.
It gives up strict consistency for speed: appends happen at least once, and the applications are written to cope with the odd duplicate.

body.x: The paper: "The Google File System" by Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff and Shun-Tak Leung, SOSP 2003.

The authors stored a crawl of the web and the indexes built from it: files of many gigabytes, written by appending and read start to finish by batch jobs. They ran on hundreds of ordinary machines with ordinary disks, and with that many machines a disk, a power supply, a switch or a bug was always failing somewhere.

items: Failures are the normal case, so finding them and recovering must be automatic.
Files are huge: a few million of them, typically 100 MB or more, most of them several gigabytes.
Most writes append to the end of a file; overwriting the middle is rare.
Reads are mostly long and sequential, so steady throughput matters more than the speed of one small read.

body.x: Zotato's order events have the same shape: every order, payment and rider ping appended to big log files all day, and nightly jobs that read them from start to finish.

items: Files are cut into 64 MB chunks. Each chunk is a plain file on three chunkservers by default, spread across racks so one failed rack doesn't take every copy.

One master keeps the whole namespace in memory: file names, which chunks make up each file, and where each chunk's copies are. That is under 64 bytes per chunk, so one machine's memory can describe petabytes.
Clients ask the master where a chunk is, cache the answer, and then talk to the chunkservers directly.

body.cap: The report job asks the master once, then reads straight from a chunkserver. The master handles a few small requests per job and never the gigabytes, which is why a single master was enough.

body.x: Writing: a lease decides the order

Three copies must apply writes in the same order, or they drift apart. The master gives one copy a lease on the chunk, 60 seconds and renewed while writes continue, and that copy becomes the primary: it numbers the writes and the others apply them in that order. If the primary vanishes, the master waits for the lease to run out before naming a new one, so there are never two primaries at once.

body.cap: Data and control travel separately. The data is pushed along a chain of servers, so each machine's network link carries it once and all three receive it at nearly the same time. Only then does the small 'write it' go to the primary, which numbers the write so every copy applies it in the same place.

body.x: The paper's favourite operation is record append: the client hands over only the data and GFS chooses the offset. Hundreds of crawler or log machines can append to one file at once without a lock. If a copy fails part-way the client retries, so a record can appear twice or leave padding behind; readers skip the padding and drop duplicates using checksums and record IDs.

items: Chunkservers send the master a heartbeat. When one goes quiet, the master copies its chunks from the surviving copies until each is back to three, most urgent first: a chunk down to one copy before a chunk down to two.
Each chunk has a version number, raised with every new lease. A server that was down while writes happened comes back with an old number, and its stale copy is deleted.
The master's state is a log of every change, copied to other machines and checkpointed. A new master can start from it, and read-only shadow masters keep reads going meanwhile.
A deleted file is only renamed and hidden; its space is reclaimed in the background three days later, which also makes a mistaken delete recoverable.

body.label: GFS trade-offs
head: Choice
What it bought
What it cost
rows: Simple, global decisions about where copies go
A ceiling on how many files fit in one machine's memory
Few master lookups and long, efficient reads
A small file read by hundreds of machines at once overloads its three servers
Fast appends from many writers at once
Applications must handle duplicates and padding

body.x: The single master was eventually the limit: as files grew into the hundreds of millions and more applications needed quick answers, its authors' company replaced GFS with a successor that spreads the metadata over many machines. Meanwhile HDFS, the open-source copy, kept the design almost exactly (a NameNode as the master, DataNodes as chunkservers) and ran on thousands of clusters.

items: For big files (videos, backups, logs), split them into chunks, keep three copies on different racks, and keep the chunk map in a metadata service. The File sync and Photo sharing problems use this shape.
Separate metadata from data: the metadata service answers 'where is it', and clients move the bytes directly to and from the storage servers.
Say how you notice a dead server (heartbeats) and how you get back to three copies.
Name the consistency you accept: GFS allows a duplicate append because readers can drop it.

body.x: Large chunks mean a job reading a 1 GB file asks the master 16 times, not thousands, and keeps one long connection to a chunkserver. The cost showed up as hot spots: a small file that fits in one chunk, such as a program that hundreds of machines start at the same moment, overloads the three servers holding it. The fix was more copies for such files and staggered start times.
